Tamper

/TAM-per/ — rhymes with hamper · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To tamper with something is to meddle with it in a way that changes, damages, or interferes with how it normally works, usually without permission.

Someone had tampered with the scoreboard, adding fifty points overnight.

Worked Example

Investigators discovered that someone had tampered with the evidence, planting false documents to frame the suspect.

Tamper captures the idea of unauthorized meddling that deliberately alters or damages something's normal function. It's not casual touching or examining—it's stealthy interference with intent to harm. The word conveys both the violation and the harmful effect.

How Tamper Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

Antonyms

preserve

preserve: to keep something safe in its original state

safeguard

safeguard: to protect something from harm or interference

How Strong Is It? — touch → adjust → tamper → sabotage

touch vs. tamper

touch vs. tamper: Touch is far weaker than tamper: touching something leaves it as it was, while tampering means meddling with it so it no longer works the way it should.

adjust vs. tamper

adjust vs. tamper: Adjust is weaker than tamper — adjusting makes careful, permitted changes, but tampering makes secret, unauthorized ones that damage or interfere.

sabotage vs. tamper

sabotage vs. tamper: Sabotage is stronger than tamper: tampering meddles with something without permission, while sabotage deliberately wrecks it to make it fail.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tamper (variant of temper)

Root — tamper (variant of temper): to mix in due proportion, to regulate (Latin (temperāre), via Middle French)

Put it together

Put it together: Tamper began as a workshop pronunciation of temper, from Latin temperāre, 'to mix in proper proportion' — workers 'tempered' clay by mixing it thoroughly. Over time, tampering with something came to mean mixing into it without permission: meddling so that it no longer works the way it should.

Use the root in a new word: temper

Use the root in a new word: temper: When a chef tempers chocolate, she mixes and adjusts it with great care — tamper comes from that very same word, but drifted to mean mixing into something you have no business changing.

Word Choice

neutral

Tamper suggests deliberate, unauthorized meddling that interferes with something's normal function or purpose. Use it when someone secretly alters or damages something they shouldn't touch. For authorized changes or minor adjustments, 'modify' or 'adjust' is more appropriate.
